claim: Present-day non-African human populations inherit 1–4% of their genetic ancestry from introgression with Neanderthals.
source: Genomic analyses have revealed that present-day non-African human populations inherit 1–4% of their genetic ancestry from introgression with Neanderthals (Green et al., 2010; Prüfer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Green et al., 2010 and Prüfer et al., 2014

claim: Neanderthal introgression introduced uniquely Neanderthal variants into the ancestral out-of-Africa human gene pool.
source: This introgression event introduced uniquely Neanderthal variants into the ancestral out-of-Africa human gene pool, which may have helped this bottleneck population survive the new environments they encountered (Mendez et al., 2012; Abi-Rached et al., 2011; Sankararaman et al., 2014; Vernot and Akey, 2014; Racimo et al., 2015; Gittelman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: Many Neanderthal variants appear to have been deleterious in the modern human genetic background leading to a reduction in Neanderthal ancestry in conserved genomic regions.
source: On the other hand, many Neanderthal variants appear to have been deleterious in the modern human genetic background leading to a reduction in Neanderthal ancestry in conserved genomic regions (Sankararaman et al., 2014; Vernot and Akey, 2014; Harris and Nielsen, 2016; Juric et al., 2016; Petr et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Some Neanderthal introgressed variants are significantly associated with traits such as skin tone, hair color, and height based on genome-wide association studies in British samples.
source: Previously, (Dannemann and Kelso, 2017) showed that some Neanderthal introgressed variants are significantly associated with traits such as skin tone, hair color, and height based on genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in British samples.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dannemann and Kelso, 2017

claim: Most of the significantly associated Neanderthal introgressed SNPs are in the proximity of strongly associated non-archaic variants.
source: However, using data from Iceland, Skov et al., 2020 found that most of the significantly associated Neanderthal introgressed single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) are in the proximity of strongly associated non-archaic variants.
evidence: Supported by citation to Skov et al., 2020

claim: Associations at Neanderthal introgressed SNPs were driven by the associations at linked non-archaic variants, indicating a limited contribution to modern human phenotypes from Neanderthal introgression.
source: They suggested that these associations at Neanderthal introgressed SNPs were driven by the associations at linked non-archaic variants, indicating a limited contribution to modern human phenotypes from Neanderthal introgression.
evidence: Supported by citation to Skov et al., 2020 in the preceding sentence

claim: McArthur et al., 2021 estimated the proportion of heritable variation that can be attributed to introgressed variants though their approach is restricted to common variants (minor allele frequency >5%).
source: A recent study by McArthur et al., 2021 estimated the proportion of heritable variation that can be attributed to introgressed variants though their approach is restricted to common variants (minor allele frequency >5%) that represent a minority of introgressed variants.
evidence: Supported by citation to McArthur et al., 2021

claim: Variants introgressed from Neanderthals are rare on average due to the low proportion of Neanderthal ancestry in present-day genomes.
source: The first challenge is that variants introgressed from Neanderthals are rare on average (due to the low proportion of Neanderthal ancestry in present-day genomes).
evidence: Inference based on the low proportion of Neanderthal ancestry

claim: Introgressed Neanderthal variants have distinct population genetic properties that can confound attempts to characterize their effects.
source: The second challenge arises from the unique evolutionary history of introgressed Neanderthal variants, resulting in distinct population genetic properties at these variants, which can, in turn, confound attempts to characterize their effects.
evidence: Inference based on the unique evolutionary history of introgressed variants

claim: 6027 SNPs were added to the UKBB genotyping array to better tag Neanderthal ancestry.
source: We iteratively chose SNPs until we obtained 6027 SNPs (requiring 16,674 features) that fully tagged the remaining set of Neanderthal-derived SNPs. These 6027 SNPs were then added to the UKBiobank Axiom array.
evidence: Description of the study's methodology

claim: 235,592 variants are likely to be Neanderthal-derived (termed Neanderthal Informative Mutations [NIMs]) out of a total of 7,774,235 QC-ed SNPs in UKBB.
source: These SNPs allow variants of Neanderthal ancestry to be confidently imputed and allow us to identify a list of 235,592 variants that are likely to be Neanderthal-derived (termed Neanderthal Informative Mutations [NIMs]) out of a total of 7,774,235 QC-ed SNPs in UKBB (see 'Methods'; Appendix 1).
evidence: Data from the study's analysis of UKBB genotypes

claim: Introgressed Neanderthal variants make a significant contribution to trait variation, explaining 0.12% of trait variation on average.
source: Introgressed Neanderthal variants make a significant contribution to trait variation (explaining 0.12% of trait variation on average).
evidence: Data from the study's heritability analysis

claim: The contribution of introgressed variants tends to be significantly depleted relative to modern human variants matched for allele frequency and linkage disequilibrium (about 59% depletion on average).
source: However, the contribution of introgressed variants tends to be significantly depleted relative to modern human variants matched for allele frequency and linkage disequilibrium (about 59% depletion on average), consistent with purifying selection on introgressed variants.
evidence: Data from the study's heritability analysis

claim: The depletion in heritability of introgressed variants is consistent with purifying selection on introgressed variants.
source: However, the contribution of introgressed variants tends to be significantly depleted relative to modern human variants matched for allele frequency and linkage disequilibrium (about 59% depletion on average), consistent with purifying selection on introgressed variants.
evidence: Inference from the observed depletion pattern

claim: There is no evidence for elevated heritability across the phenotypes examined, different from previous studies.
source: Different from previous studies (McArthur et al., 2021), we find no evidence for elevated heritability across the phenotypes examined.
evidence: Data from the study's heritability analysis

claim: 348 independent significant associations of introgressed Neanderthal variants with 64 phenotypes were identified.
source: We identified 348 independent significant associations of introgressed Neanderthal variants with 64 phenotypes.
evidence: Data from the study's association testing

claim: A majority of associations of introgressed variants with phenotypes are likely driven by statistical association with nearby modern human variants that are the true causal variants.
source: Previous work (Skov et al., 2020) has suggested that a majority of such associations are likely driven by statistical association with nearby modern human variants that are the true causal variants.
evidence: Supported by citation to Skov et al., 2020

claim: 112 regions across 47 phenotypes containing 4303 unique genetic variants were identified where introgressed variants are highly likely to have a phenotypic effect.
source: Applying a customized fine-mapping led us to identify 112 regions across 47 phenotypes containing 4303 unique genetic variants where introgressed variants are highly likely to have a phenotypic effect.
evidence: Data from the study's fine-mapping analysis

claim: Credible NIMs have substantial impact on genes that are important for the immune system, development, and metabolism.
source: Examination of these variants reveals their substantial impact on genes that are important for the immune system, development, and metabolism.
evidence: Data from functional annotation of credible NIMs

claim: NIMs tend to have lower MAF compared to MH SNPs.
source: We observe that NIMs tend to have lower MAF (Figure 2a) and higher LD scores compared to MH SNPs (Figure 2b) (the average MAF of NIMs and MH SNPs are 3.9% and 9.9%, respectively, while their average LD scores are 170.6 and 64.9).
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes shown in Figure 2a

claim: NIMs tend to have higher LD scores compared to MH SNPs.
source: We observe that NIMs tend to have lower MAF (Figure 2a) and higher LD scores compared to MH SNPs (Figure 2b) (the average MAF of NIMs and MH SNPs are 3.9% and 9.9%, respectively, while their average LD scores are 170.6 and 64.9).
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes shown in Figure 2b

claim: The average MAF of NIMs is 3.9% and the average MAF of MH SNPs is 9.9%.
source: We observe that NIMs tend to have lower MAF (Figure 2a) and higher LD scores compared to MH SNPs (Figure 2b) (the average MAF of NIMs and MH SNPs are 3.9% and 9.9%, respectively, while their average LD scores are 170.6 and 64.9).
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes

claim: The average LD score of NIMs is 170.6 and the average LD score of MH SNPs is 64.9.
source: We observe that NIMs tend to have lower MAF (Figure 2a) and higher LD scores compared to MH SNPs (Figure 2b) (the average MAF of NIMs and MH SNPs are 3.9% and 9.9%, respectively, while their average LD scores are 170.6 and 64.9).
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes

claim: 76.9% of NIMs have MAF >1%.
source: Among the QC-ed SNPs, 76.9% of NIMs have MAF >1%, and 27.7% have MAF >5%, in contrast to 61.6% and 41.6% of MH SNPs.
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes

claim: 27.7% of NIMs have MAF >5%.
source: Among the QC-ed SNPs, 76.9% of NIMs have MAF >1%, and 27.7% have MAF >5%, in contrast to 61.6% and 41.6% of MH SNPs.
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes

claim: 61.6% of MH SNPs have MAF >1%.
source: Among the QC-ed SNPs, 76.9% of NIMs have MAF >1%, and 27.7% have MAF >5%, in contrast to 61.6% and 41.6% of MH SNPs.
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes

claim: 41.6% of MH SNPs have MAF >5%.
source: Among the QC-ed SNPs, 76.9% of NIMs have MAF >1%, and 27.7% have MAF >5%, in contrast to 61.6% and 41.6% of MH SNPs.
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes

claim: The MAF and LD score of NIMs tend not to increase with each other, distinct from MH SNPs.
source: Distinct from MH SNPs, the MAF and LD score of NIMs tend not to increase with each other (Figure 2cd).
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes shown in Figure 2c and 2d

claim: Not accounting for either MAF or LD leads to poor calibration in heritability estimation.
source: On the other hand, not accounting for either MAF or LD leads to poor calibration (Figure 1; we observe qualitatively similar results when estimating genome-wide SNP heritability; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from simulations shown in Figure 1

claim: 17 phenotypes show significant evidence of depleted NIM heritability including standing height, body mass index, and HDL cholesterol.
source: We find 17 phenotypes with significant evidence of depleted NIM heritability that include standing height, body mass index, and HDL cholesterol (Z-score < –3; Figure 3b and d).
evidence: Data from RHE-mc analysis of UKBB phenotypes shown in Figure 3b and 3d

claim: Five phenotypic categories show significant NIM heritability depletion: anthropometry, blood biochemistry, blood pressure, lipid metabolism, and lung.
source: Five phenotypic categories show significant NIM heritability depletion (anthropometry, blood biochemistry, blood pressure, lipid metabolism, lung) in meta-analysis.
evidence: Data from meta-analysis of UKBB phenotypes

claim: Heritability at NIMs is reduced by about 57% relative to an MH variant with matched MAF and LD characteristics.
source: On average, we find that heritability at NIMs is reduced by about 57% relative to an MH variant with matched MAF and LD characteristics.
evidence: Data from RHE-mc analysis of UKBB phenotypes

claim: There is no evidence for traits with elevated NIM heritability across the phenotypes analyzed.
source: In contrast to the evidence for depletion in NIM heritability, we find no evidence for traits with elevated NIM heritability across the phenotypes analyzed.
evidence: Data from RHE-mc analysis of UKBB phenotypes

claim: The observations are consistent with NIMs having been primarily under purifying selection for thousands of generations.
source: Our observations are consistent with NIMs having been primarily under purifying selection for thousands of generations (Harris and Nielsen, 2016; Petr et al., 2019).
evidence: Inference from the observed depletion pattern, supported by citations

claim: NIMs still make a significant contribution to phenotypic variation in present-day humans as evidenced by their overall heritability.
source: Nevertheless, as evidenced by their overall heritability, NIMs still make a significant contribution to phenotypic variation in present-day humans.
evidence: Inference from the observed positive NIM heritability

claim: Analyses that do not control for MAF and LD underestimate both heritability and NIM heritability.
source: However, these analyses underestimate both heritability (Figure 4a) and NIM heritability (Figure 4b), resulting in apparent NIM heritability depletion (Z-score < –3) in 83 of the 96 phenotypes (Figure 4c).
evidence: Data from comparison of methods shown in Figure 4

claim: Not controlling for MAF and LD results in apparent NIM heritability depletion in 83 of the 96 phenotypes.
source: However, these analyses underestimate both heritability (Figure 4a) and NIM heritability (Figure 4b), resulting in apparent NIM heritability depletion (Z-score < –3) in 83 of the 96 phenotypes (Figure 4c).
evidence: Data from comparison of methods shown in Figure 4c

claim: The depletion in heritability likely reflects selection against Neanderthal alleles rather than selection against variation in functionally constrained regions of the genome in general.
source: Taken together, our analyses suggest that depletion in heritability likely reflects selection against Neanderthal alleles rather than selection against variation in functionally constrained regions of the genome in general.
evidence: Inference from analysis matching on B-values

claim: A total of 13,075 significant NIM-phenotype associations in 64 phenotypes with 8018 unique NIMs were obtained (p<10–10).
source: We obtained a total of 13,075 significant NIM-phenotype associations in 64 phenotypes with 8018 unique NIMs (p<10–10 that accounts for the number of SNPs and phenotypes tested) from which we obtain 348 significant NIM-phenotype associations with 294 unique NIMs after clumping associated NIMs by LD (see 'Methods).
evidence: Data from association testing of UKBB phenotypes

claim: After clumping associated NIMs by LD, 348 significant NIM-phenotype associations with 294 unique NIMs were obtained.
source: We obtained a total of 13,075 significant NIM-phenotype associations in 64 phenotypes with 8018 unique NIMs (p<10–10 that accounts for the number of SNPs and phenotypes tested) from which we obtain 348 significant NIM-phenotype associations with 294 unique NIMs after clumping associated NIMs by LD (see 'Methods).
evidence: Data from association testing of UKBB phenotypes

claim: The false discovery proportion of the association testing approach is around 30% across all genetic architectures.
source: Averaging across all genetic architectures, the false discovery proportion (FDP; the fraction of false positives among the significant NIMs) of the association testing approach is around 30% (Figure 5b).
evidence: Data from simulations shown in Figure 5b

claim: Finding NIMs that are significantly associated with a phenotype does not confidently localize regions at which introgressed variants affect phenotypes.
source: Hence, finding NIMs that are significantly associated with a phenotype does not confidently localize regions at which introgressed variants affect phenotypes.
evidence: Inference from the high false discovery proportion of association testing

claim: The fine mapping approach yields a reduction in the FDP relative to association mapping (FDP of 15.6% on average).
source: The fine mapping approach yields a reduction in the FDP relative to association mapping (FDP of 15.6% on average; Figure 5b) while attributing the causal effect to a few dozen NIMs within the credible NIM set (mean: 79, median: 54 NIMs across all simulations).
evidence: Data from simulations shown in Figure 5b

claim: The fine mapping approach attributes the causal effect to a mean of 79 and median of 54 NIMs within the credible NIM set across all simulations.
source: The fine mapping approach yields a reduction in the FDP relative to association mapping (FDP of 15.6% on average; Figure 5b) while attributing the causal effect to a few dozen NIMs within the credible NIM set (mean: 79, median: 54 NIMs across all simulations).
evidence: Data from simulations

claim: A total of 112 credible NIM regions containing 4303 unique credible NIMs across 47 phenotypes were identified.
source: Applying our pipeline to the set of 96 UKBB phenotypes, we identified a total of 112 credible NIM regions containing 4303 unique credible NIMs across 47 phenotypes (Figure 6a).
evidence: Data from fine-mapping analysis of UKBB phenotypes shown in Figure 6a

claim: The median length of credible NIM regions is 65.7 kb (95% CI: [4.41 kb, 469.3 kb]).
source: The median length of credible NIM regions, 65.7 kb (95% CI: [4.41 kb, 469.3 kb]) is close to the expected length of Neanderthal introgressed segments (Skov et al., 2020) suggesting that the resolution of our approach is that of an introgressed LD block (Figure 5c).
evidence: Data from fine-mapping analysis shown in Figure 5c

claim: The median length of credible NIM regions is close to the expected length of Neanderthal introgressed segments, suggesting that the resolution of the approach is that of an introgressed LD block.
source: The median length of credible NIM regions, 65.7 kb (95% CI: [4.41 kb, 469.3 kb]) is close to the expected length of Neanderthal introgressed segments (Skov et al., 2020) suggesting that the resolution of our approach is that of an introgressed LD block (Figure 5c).
evidence: Inference from comparison with expected segment length, supported by citation to Skov et al., 2020

claim: Fine mapping generally attributes the causal signal to a mean of 55.8 and median of 37 NIMs across phenotypes.
source: While fine mapping generally attributes the causal signal to a subset of the tested NIMs (mean: 55.8, median: 37 NIMs across phenotypes), the degree of this reduction varies across regions likely reflecting differences in the LD among NIMs (Figure 5d).
evidence: Data from fine-mapping analysis shown in Figure 5d

claim: No credible NIM was detected in 49 out of 96 phenotypes potentially due to the limited power of the procedure.
source: We do not detect any credible NIM in 49 out of 96 phenotypes potentially due to the limited power of our procedure that aims to control the FDR (Figure 5e).
evidence: Data from fine-mapping analysis shown in Figure 5e

claim: The sensitivity of the fine-mapping method is affected by both total heritability (Pearson's r = 0.49, p=3.3×10–7) and NIM heritability (Pearson's r = 0.36, p=3.3×10–4).
source: The sensitivity of our method is affected by both total heritability (Figure 5f, Pearson's r = 0.49, p=3.3×10–7) and NIM heritability (Figure 5g, Pearson's r = 0.36, p=3.3×10–4).
evidence: Data from correlation analysis shown in Figure 5f and 5g

claim: A linear model using both total heritability and NIM heritability to predict the number of credible sets yields r2 = 0.29, p=1.3×10–5 and 0.015, respectively.
source: A linear model that uses both total heritability and NIM heritability to predict the number of credible sets yields r2 = 0.29, p=1.3×10–5 and 0.015, respectively, while linear models with only total heritability or only NIM heritability result in statistically lower r2 (0.24 and 0.13, respectively).
evidence: Data from linear regression analysis

claim: A total of 26 credible NIMs have high or moderate impact on genes.
source: We annotated all 4303 unique credible NIMs using SnpEff (Cingolani et al., 2012) to identify a total of 26 NIMs with high (e.g., start codon loss, stop codon gain) or moderate impact (nonsynonymous variants) on genes (Figure 6b).
evidence: Data from functional annotation shown in Figure 6b

claim: Two credible NIMs, rs9427397 (1:161,476,204 C>T) and rs60542959 (12:56,660,905 G>T), have a high impact on protein sequences.
source: We identified two credible NIMs, rs9427397 (1:161,476,204 C>T) and rs60542959 (12:56,660,905 G>T), that have a high impact on protein sequences.
evidence: Data from functional annotation

claim: The 1:161,476,204 C>T mutation introduces a premature stop codon in the FCGR2A gene.
source: The 1:161,476,204 C>T mutation, an NIM that is associated with increased gamma glutamyltransferase and aspartate aminotransferase (enzymes associated with liver function) and decreased total protein levels in blood, introduces a premature stop codon in the FCGR2A gene (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from functional annotation shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The 1:161,476,204 C>T mutation is associated with increased gamma glutamyltransferase and aspartate aminotransferase and decreased total protein levels in blood.
source: The 1:161,476,204 C>T mutation, an NIM that is associated with increased gamma glutamyltransferase and aspartate aminotransferase (enzymes associated with liver function) and decreased total protein levels in blood, introduces a premature stop codon in the FCGR2A gene (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Data from association testing shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: FCGR2A codes for a receptor in many immune cells, such as macrophages and neutrophils, and is involved in the process of phagocytosis and clearing of immune complexes.
source: FCGR2A codes for a receptor in many immune cells, such as macrophages and neutrophils, and is involved in the process of phagocytosis and clearing of immune complexes.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about FCGR2A function

claim: The 1:161,476,204 C>T mutation is in a region that contains SNPs shown in several GWAS linked to rheumatoid arthritis.
source: This NIM is in a region that contains SNPs shown in several GWAS linked to rheumatoid arthritis (Okada et al., 2014; Laufer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okada et al., 2014 and Laufer et al., 2019

claim: The 12:56,660,905 G>T (rs60542959) mutation results in the loss of the start codon in COQ10A.
source: The other high-impact mutation, 12:56,660,905 G>T (rs60542959), results in the loss of the start codon in COQ10A, and this SNP is a credible NIM for both mean platelet volume and standing height (Figure 6c).
evidence: Data from functional annotation shown in Figure 6c

claim: rs60542959 is a credible NIM for both mean platelet volume and standing height.
source: The other high-impact mutation, 12:56,660,905 G>T (rs60542959), results in the loss of the start codon in COQ10A, and this SNP is a credible NIM for both mean platelet volume and standing height (Figure 6c).
evidence: Data from fine-mapping analysis shown in Figure 6c

claim: COQ10 genes (A and B) are important in respiratory chain reactions.
source: COQ10 genes (A and B) are important in respiratory chain reactions.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about COQ10 function

claim: Deficiencies of CoQ10 have been associated with encephalomyopathy, infantile multisystemic disease; cerebellar ataxia, and pure myopathy.
source: Deficiencies of CoQ10 (MIM 607426) have been associated with encephalomyopathy, infantile multisystemic disease; cerebellar ataxia, and pure myopathy (Quinzii et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quinzii et al., 2008

claim: The start codon in COQ10A is conserved among mammals.
source: The start codon in COQ10A is conserved among mammals with its loss having a potentially significant effect on COQ10A expression in immune cells (Kubota and Suyama, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kubota and Suyama, 2020

claim: Loss of the start codon in COQ10A has a potentially significant effect on COQ10A expression in immune cells.
source: The start codon in COQ10A is conserved among mammals with its loss having a potentially significant effect on COQ10A expression in immune cells (Kubota and Suyama, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kubota and Suyama, 2020

claim: 24 credible NIMs function as missense mutations in 19 genes.
source: In addition, we detect 24 credible NIMs that function as missense mutations in 19 genes.
evidence: Data from functional annotation

claim: Seven out of the 19 genes with missense credible NIMs are known to have immune related functions (FCGR2A, PCDHG (A8, A9, B7, C4), STAT2, and IKZF3).
source: Seven out of the 19 genes are known to have immune related functions (FCGR2A, PCDHG (A8, A9, B7, C4), STAT2, and IKZF3).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about gene functions

claim: The NIM in STAT2 (rs2066807, 12:56,740,682 C>G) was the first adaptive introgression locus to be identified.
source: The NIM in STAT2 (rs2066807, 12:56,740,682 C>G) was the first adaptive introgression locus to be identified (Mendez et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mendez et al., 2012

claim: The STAT2 introgressed variant segregates at 0.066 frequency in the UKBB white British.
source: The STAT2 introgressed variant segregates at 0.066 frequency in the UKBB white British and leads to an I594M amino acid change in the corresponding protein.
evidence: Data from UKBB genotypes

claim: The STAT2 introgressed variant leads to an I594M amino acid change in the corresponding protein.
source: The STAT2 introgressed variant segregates at 0.066 frequency in the UKBB white British and leads to an I594M amino acid change in the corresponding protein.
evidence: Data from functional annotation

claim: STAT2 gene and COQ10A are neighboring genes, providing an example of an introgressed region that potentially impacts function at multiple genes.
source: STAT2 gene and COQ10A are neighboring genes, thereby providing an example of an introgressed region that potentially impacts function at multiple genes (Figure 6c).
evidence: Data from genomic location shown in Figure 6c

claim: At least 7 of the 12 genes with missense credible NIMs not known to be immune related have other important functions documented in the literature, such as DNA replication/damage (FANCA, CCDC8), transition in meiosis (FBXO34), detoxification/metabolism (AKR1C4), and neurological/developmental (ZNF778, ANKRD11, TBC1D32) functions.
source: At least 7 of the 12 genes not known to be immune related have other important functions documented in the literature, such as DNA replication/damage (FANCA, CCDC8) (Moldovan and D'Andrea, 2009; Jiang et al., 2016), transition in meiosis (FBXO34) (Zhao et al., 2021), detoxification/metabolism (AKR1C4) (Lee et al., 2009), and neurological/developmental (ZNF778, ANKRD11, TBC1D32) functions (Willemsen et al., 2010; Alves et al., 2019; Hietamäki et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: rs17134592 (10:5260682 C>G) is a non-synonymous mutation in AKR1C4, a gene that is involved in the metabolism of ketone-containing steroids in the liver.
source: rs17134592 (10:5260682 C>G) is a non-synonymous mutation in AKR1C4, a gene that is involved in the metabolism of ketone-containing steroids in the liver.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about AKR1C4 function

claim: rs17134592 is associated with increased serum bilirubin levels (p=3×10–11).
source: The NIM is associated with increased serum bilirubin levels (p=3×10–11) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a) while also being associated with increased levels of alkaline phosphatase, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) and decreased apolipoprotein A, sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and triglyceride levels.
evidence: Data from association testing shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a

claim: rs17134592 is associated with increased levels of alkaline phosphatase and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) and decreased apolipoprotein A, sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and triglyceride levels.
source: The NIM is associated with increased serum bilirubin levels (p=3×10–11) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a) while also being associated with increased levels of alkaline phosphatase, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) and decreased apolipoprotein A, sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and triglyceride levels.
evidence: Data from association testing

claim: rs17134592 has been identified to be a splicing QTL that is active in the liver and testis in the GTEx data.
source: rs17134592 has been identified to be a splicing QTL that is active in the liver and testis in the GTeX data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Data from GTEx shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b

claim: rs17134592 alters leucine to valine (L311V).
source: This NIM alters leucine to valine (L311V), which, in combination with the tightly linked non-synonymous variant rs3829125 (S145C) in the same gene, have been shown to confer a three- to fivefold reduction in catalytic activity of the corresponding enzyme (3-alpha hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase) in human liver (Kume et al., 1999).
evidence: Data from functional annotation

claim: rs17134592 (L311V) in combination with rs3829125 (S145C) confer a three- to fivefold reduction in catalytic activity of 3-alpha hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase in human liver.
source: This NIM alters leucine to valine (L311V), which, in combination with the tightly linked non-synonymous variant rs3829125 (S145C) in the same gene, have been shown to confer a three- to fivefold reduction in catalytic activity of the corresponding enzyme (3-alpha hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase) in human liver (Kume et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kume et al., 1999

claim: The single amino acid change S145C did not significantly alter enzyme activity, suggesting the importance of the amino acid residue at position 311 for the substrate binding of the enzyme.
source: Interestingly, the single amino acid change S145C did not significantly alter enzyme activity, suggesting the importance of the amino acid residue at position 311 for the substrate binding of the enzyme.
evidence: Inference from the observation that S145C alone does not alter activity

claim: 60.8% of the credible NIMs are eQTLs for at least one gene in at least one tissue.
source: We find that 60.8% of the credible NIMs are eQTLs for at least one gene in at least one tissue while only 25.6% of all NIMs are eQTLs.
evidence: Data from eQTL annotation using GTEx v8

claim: Only 25.6% of all NIMs are eQTLs.
source: We find that 60.8% of the credible NIMs are eQTLs for at least one gene in at least one tissue while only 25.6% of all NIMs are eQTLs.
evidence: Data from eQTL annotation using GTEx v8

claim: Out of 112 credible NIM sets, 23 have at least one credible NIM that alters coding sequence.
source: Out of 112 credible NIM sets, 23 have at least one credible NIM that alters coding sequence (Figure 6b), 79 have at least one credible NIM that works as an eQTL in at least one tissue while 22 have at least one credible NIM that impacts both coding sequence and gene expression.
evidence: Data from functional annotation shown in Figure 6b

claim: Out of 112 credible NIM sets, 79 have at least one credible NIM that works as an eQTL in at least one tissue.
source: Out of 112 credible NIM sets, 23 have at least one credible NIM that alters coding sequence (Figure 6b), 79 have at least one credible NIM that works as an eQTL in at least one tissue while 22 have at least one credible NIM that impacts both coding sequence and gene expression.
evidence: Data from functional annotation

claim: Out of 112 credible NIM sets, 22 have at least one credible NIM that impacts both coding sequence and gene expression.
source: Out of 112 credible NIM sets, 23 have at least one credible NIM that alters coding sequence (Figure 6b), 79 have at least one credible NIM that works as an eQTL in at least one tissue while 22 have at least one credible NIM that impacts both coding sequence and gene expression.
evidence: Data from functional annotation

claim: The credible set for measures of lung capacity (FEV1 and FVC) contains eQTLs for genes expressed in lung.
source: We find examples of credible NIMs for specific phenotypes that are eQTLs in relevant tissues: the credible set for measures of lung capacity (forced expiratory volume [FEV1] and forced vital capacity [FVC]) contains eQTLs for gene expressed in lung while credible sets for a measure of liver function (alanine aminotransferase levels in blood) contain eQTLs in liver.
evidence: Data from eQTL annotation

claim: Credible sets for a measure of liver function (alanine aminotransferase levels in blood) contain eQTLs in liver.
source: We find examples of credible NIMs for specific phenotypes that are eQTLs in relevant tissues: the credible set for measures of lung capacity (forced expiratory volume [FEV1] and forced vital capacity [FVC]) contains eQTLs for gene expressed in lung while credible sets for a measure of liver function (alanine aminotransferase levels in blood) contain eQTLs in liver.
evidence: Data from eQTL annotation

claim: The overall contribution of introgressed Neanderthal alleles to phenotypic variation indicates a pattern where these alleles tend to be depleted in their impact on phenotypic variation.
source: The assessment of the overall contribution of introgressed Neanderthal alleles to phenotypic variation indicates a pattern where, taken as a group, these alleles tend to be depleted in their impact on phenotypic variation (with about a third of the studied phenotypes showing evidence of depletion).
evidence: Data from heritability analysis

claim: About a third of the studied phenotypes show evidence of depletion in the impact of introgressed alleles on phenotypic variation.
source: The assessment of the overall contribution of introgressed Neanderthal alleles to phenotypic variation indicates a pattern where, taken as a group, these alleles tend to be depleted in their impact on phenotypic variation (with about a third of the studied phenotypes showing evidence of depletion).
evidence: Data from heritability analysis

claim: The pattern of depletion is consistent with introgressed alleles having entered the modern human population roughly 50,000 years ago and being subject to purifying selection.
source: This pattern is consistent with these alleles having entered the modern human population roughly 50,000 y ago and being subject to purifying selection.
evidence: Inference from the observed depletion pattern

claim: Selection to purify deleterious introgressed variants, coupled with stabilizing selection on human complex traits, could result in introgressed heritability depletion such that the remaining introgressed variants in present-day humans tend to have smaller phenotypic effects compared to other modern human variants.
source: Selection to purify deleterious introgressed variants, coupled with stabilizing selection on human complex traits, could result in introgressed heritability depletion such that the remaining introgressed variants in present-day humans tend to have smaller phenotypic effects compared to other modern human variants.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary mechanisms

claim: The discrepancy with McArthur et al., 2021 could be due to the different methods and NIMs used in the two studies.
source: In contrast to the previous heritability analyses by McArthur et al., 2021, we did not find any NIM heritability enrichment in the 96 phenotypes. This discrepancy could be due to the different methods and NIMs used in the two studies.
evidence: Speculation about reasons for discrepancy

claim: McArthur et al. estimate the heritability associated with common NIMs (NIMs with MAF >5%) using stratified LD score regression with LD scores computed from 1KG.
source: McArthur et al. estimate the heritability associated with common NIMs (NIMs with MAF >5%) using stratified LD score regression (S-LDSR) with LD scores computed from 1KG (see Appendix 2).
evidence: Description of McArthur et al.'s methods

claim: More than 70% of NIMs have MAF <5%.
source: Because more than 70% of NIMs have MAF <5%, this approach may not extrapolate to understand the heritability from all NIMs.
evidence: Data from analysis of UKBB genotypes

claim: The approach of McArthur et al. may not extrapolate to understand the heritability from all NIMs because more than 70% of NIMs have MAF <5%.
source: Because more than 70% of NIMs have MAF <5%, this approach may not extrapolate to understand the heritability from all NIMs.
evidence: Inference from the limitation of analyzing only common NIMs

claim: Typical approaches to account for population stratification based on the inclusion of principal components may not be adequate as these PCs are computed from common SNPs and may not account for stratification at the NIMs that tend to be rare on average.
source: Typical approaches to account for population stratification based on the inclusion of principal components (PCs) may not be adequate as these PCs are computed from common SNPs on the UKBB genotyping array and may not account for stratification at the NIMs that tend to be rare on average (Mathieson and McVean, 2012).
evidence: Inference supported by citation to Mathieson and McVean, 2012

claim: The study's analyses work directly on individual genotype data and are better able to control for stratification specific to NIMs by including PCs estimated from NIMs in addition to PCs estimated from common SNPs.
source: Since our analyses work directly on individual genotype data, we are better able to control for stratification specific to NIMs by including PCs estimated from NIMs in addition to PCs estimated from common SNPs (with the caveat that even this approach is not guaranteed to correct for some types of stratification that can impact NIMs).
evidence: Description of the study's methodology

claim: The observation of an overall pattern of depletion in the heritability of introgressed alleles is consistent with the findings of McArthur et al.
source: In spite of these differences in methods and NIMs analyzed, our observation of an overall pattern of depletion in the heritability of introgressed alleles is consistent with the findings of McArthur et al.
evidence: Comparison with prior study

claim: The robustness of the depletion pattern might provide insights into the nature of selection against introgressed alleles.
source: The robustness of this pattern might provide insights into the nature of selection against introgressed alleles.
evidence: Speculation about implications

claim: NIMs tend to have lower MAF and higher LD compared to MH SNPs, which limits the power to detect a genetic effect and makes it harder to identify the causal variant.
source: A challenge in identifying such variants comes from the fact that NIMs tend to have lower MAF and higher LD compared to MH SNPs. Lower MAF tends to limit the power to detect a genetic effect while higher LD makes it harder to identify the causal variant.
evidence: Inference from the population genetic properties of NIMs

claim: The credible NIMs reported in the study offer a starting point for detailed investigation of the biological effects of introgressed variants.
source: As many of the genes are relevant to immune, metabolic, and developmental disorders, with functions relevant to the transition to new environments, the credible NIMs reported in our study offer a starting point for detailed investigation of the biological effects of introgressed variants.
evidence: Inference from the functional annotation of credible NIMs

claim: Greenbaum et al. hypothesized that introgression-based transmission of alleles related to the immune system could have helped human out-of-Africa expansion in the presence of new pathogens.
source: Greenbaum et al. hypothesized that introgression-based transmission of alleles related to the immune system could have helped human out-of-Africa expansion in the presence of new pathogens (Greenbaum et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Greenbaum et al., 2019

claim: The results do not directly support the hypothesis that introgression-based transmission of alleles related to the immune system helped human out-of-Africa expansion, but they pinpoint introgressed alleles in immune-related genes that could have and continue to modulate human phenotypes.
source: While our results do not directly support this hypothesis, they pinpoint introgressed alleles in immune-related genes that could have and continue to modulate human phenotypes consistent with findings from prior studies (Abi-Rached et al., 2011; Mendez et al., 2012; Quach et al., 2016; Nédélec et al., 2016; Enard and Petrov, 2018).
evidence: Inference from the study's findings, supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The fine-mapping strategy likely only picks up a small fraction of the functional NIMs, suggesting that additional NIMs that are causal for specific traits remain to be discovered.
source: Although we identified a number of likely causal NIMs in fine mapping, our strategy likely only picks up a small fraction of the functional NIMs, suggesting that additional NIMs that are causal for specific traits remain to be discovered.
evidence: Inference from the limited sensitivity of the fine-mapping approach

claim: All analyses focus on the white British individuals in the UKBB due to the large sample size that permits the interrogation of low-frequency NIMs and the choice of NIMs based on introgressed variants segregating in European populations.
source: First, all of our analyses focus on the white British individuals in the UKBB due to the large sample size that permits the interrogation of low-frequency NIMs and our choice of NIMs based on introgressed variants segregating in European populations.
evidence: Description of the study's limitations

claim: Whole-genome sequencing data in diverse populations can potentially elucidate the impact of Neanderthal introgression in other out-of-African populations that harbor substantial Neanderthal ancestry.
source: Whole-genome sequencing data in diverse populations can potentially elucidate the impact of Neanderthal introgression in other out-of-African populations that harbor substantial Neanderthal ancestry.
evidence: Speculation about future directions

claim: Designing arrays that have SNPs informative of archaic ancestry followed by genotype imputation could be a fruitful strategy to leverage large Biobanks to systematically explore the contribution of archaic introgression.
source: Alternatively, designing arrays that have SNPs informative of archaic ancestry followed by genotype imputation could be a fruitful strategy to leverage large Biobanks to systematically explore the contribution of archaic introgression.
evidence: Speculation about future directions

claim: The findings of lower per-SNP heritability at NIMs relative to MH SNPs are consistent with two non-exclusive hypotheses: that introgressed variants tend to have a lower proportion of causal SNPs or lower effect sizes compared to non-introgressed variants.
source: Second, our findings of lower per-SNP heritability at NIMs relative to MH SNPs are consistent with two non-exclusive hypotheses: that introgressed variants tend to have a lower proportion of causal SNPs or lower effect sizes compared to non-introgressed variants.
evidence: Inference from the observed depletion

claim: The heritability estimation approach cannot distinguish between the hypotheses that introgressed variants have a lower proportion of causal SNPs or lower effect sizes, but recent approaches that enable estimation of polygenicity of complex traits hold promise in this regard.
source: While our approach, based on heritability estimation, cannot distinguish these hypotheses, recent approaches that enable estimation of polygenicity of complex traits hold promise in this regard (Zhang et al., 2018; Johnson et al., 2021; O'Connor, 2021).
evidence: Speculation about future directions, supported by citations

claim: The design of fine mapping methods to study introgressed variants while taking into account the ancestry is an important direction for future work.
source: The design of fine mapping methods to study introgressed variants while taking into account the ancestry (as well as better incorporating other measures such as posterior inclusion probabilities) is an important direction for future work.
evidence: Speculation about future directions

claim: The unique evolutionary history of introgressed variants motivate the development of methods tailored to their population genetic properties.
source: More broadly, the unique evolutionary history of introgressed variants motivate the development of methods tailored to their population genetic properties.
evidence: Inference from the challenges encountered in the study

claim: Evolutionary models that can comprehensively explain the observations of depleted heritability at introgressed alleles are lacking.
source: While our results suggest potential evolutionary models that explain our observations of depleted heritability at introgressed alleles, evolutionary models that can comprehensively explain our observations are lacking.
evidence: Acknowledgment of limitations in current understanding

claim: Proposing and validating evolutionary models that explain the observations will be an important direction for future work.
source: Nevertheless, proposing and validating such models will be an important direction for future work.
evidence: Speculation about future directions
